questions.stem: What kind of response is a reflex?

options.explanation: Reflex responses are involuntary — automatic and rapid.
Reflexes are built in, not trained.
Speed is the defining advantage.
The conscious brain is not involved in coordinating reflexes.

questions.stem: When do you become aware that a reflex has happened?

options.explanation: No decision precedes a reflex.

options.text: After the response has already been carried out
options.explanation: Awareness follows the action in a reflex.

options.text: At the exact moment of detection
options.explanation: Detection triggers the arc, not conscious awareness.

options.text: You never become aware of reflexes
options.explanation: Awareness does arrive — just late.

questions.stem: Which structure coordinates a reflex action?

options.explanation: Receptors detect; coordination happens centrally.

options.text: The conscious part of the brain
options.explanation: Explicitly not the coordinator in a reflex.
The spinal cord acts as the reflex coordinator.
Effectors carry out the response; they do not coordinate.

questions.stem: Which trio names reflex responses correctly?

options.explanation: Those are voluntary actions.
Only some of these fit; healing is not a reflex.
All learned, conscious skills.
Those are the note's three named reflexes.

options.text: Their speed minimises damage to the body
options.explanation: Fast automatic action limits injury and aids survival.

options.text: They use less energy than thinking
options.explanation: Energy saving is not the named advantage.
Reflexes bypass the conscious brain entirely.
Sensation is irrelevant to the survival mechanism.

questions.stem: State the term for a response that does not involve the conscious brain.
questions.modelAnswer: A reflex response, also called an involuntary response.

questions.stem: Give two named examples of reflex responses.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: blinking, coughing, pain-withdrawal.

questions.stem: Explain why it is an advantage that reflex awareness comes late.
questions.modelAnswer: Waiting for conscious awareness would add decision time to every danger; by coordinating in the spinal cord and acting first, the body removes the harmful stimulus — pulling away from a flame or blinking at debris — before injury can develop, and you can think about it afterwards.

questions.stem: Dust blows toward someone's open eye. Name the reflex that protects it and describe what the body does automatically.
questions.modelAnswer: The blinking reflex protects the eye: receptors detect the irritation, the arc runs automatically, and the eyelid muscles snap the lids shut before the conscious brain has registered the dust.

questions.stem: What detects the pin-prick stimulus in the withdrawal reflex?

options.explanation: Detection happens in the skin, below conscious level.

options.text: A receptor in the skin of the foot
options.explanation: Pain, pressure or touch receptors in the skin detect the pin.

options.text: A relay neurone in the spinal cord
options.explanation: Relay neurones pass signals on; they sit mid-pathway.
The muscle is the effector at the end.

questions.stem: Which neurone carries the impulse away from the spinal cord toward the muscle?

options.explanation: Sensory neurones carry signals inward.
Relay neurones work inside the spinal cord.
The motor neurone runs the impulse out to the effector.
No such cell exists in this pathway.

questions.stem: Where does the relay neurone sit?

options.text: In the skin beside the receptor
options.explanation: Receptors connect to sensory neurones, not relays.
Muscles contain effectors, not relay neurones.
The conscious brain is bypassed in reflexes.

options.text: In the spinal cord, part of the central nervous system
options.explanation: Relay neurones are located in the CNS.

questions.stem: What does the effector do at the end of the arc?

options.text: The muscle contracts and pulls the limb away from danger
options.explanation: Contraction of the effector muscle produces the response.

options.text: It sends a second impulse to the brain
options.explanation: Effectors act; they do not relay signals.

options.text: It releases neurotransmitters into the skin
options.explanation: Neurotransmitters belong at synapses, not effector action.

options.text: It stores the impulse for later use
options.explanation: Impulses are executed immediately.

questions.stem: Why can the whole electrical pathway run so rapidly?

options.text: Because the conscious brain debates the options first
options.explanation: That would make it slow — the brain is bypassed.

options.text: Because the whole electrical pathway is short and runs without conscious thought
options.explanation: A brief spinal route plus automaticity gives speed.

options.text: Because hormones carry the signal swiftly
options.explanation: Reflexes are electrical, not hormonal.

options.text: Because muscles move faster than nerves
options.explanation: Nerve impulses set the pace; muscles merely obey.

questions.modelAnswer: The route that electrical impulses follow during a reflex action.

questions.stem: List the three neurone types in the order an impulse meets them.
questions.modelAnswer: Sensory neurone, then relay neurone, then motor neurone.

questions.stem: Explain why the spinal cord, rather than the conscious brain, serves as the coordinator here.
questions.modelAnswer: Routing the signal through the conscious brain would add perception and decision steps, delaying the withdrawal; the spinal cord sits close to the pathway, can synapse the sensory input straight to a motor output, and coordinates the rescue before injury deepens.

questions.stem: A walker's finger touches a hot object and jerks back. Write the six-stage sequence from stimulus to response for this withdrawal reflex.
questions.modelAnswer: Receptors in the finger skin detect the heat; a sensory neurone sends impulses to the spinal cord; a relay neurone receives them; the relay synapses with a motor neurone; the motor neurone carries the impulse to the arm muscles; the muscles contract and pull the finger away.
